Hmm, that seems a bit confusing at first glance. Let me break it down. First, the person is saying they "deserve" to attend the ceremony. That implies they feel entitled to be there. But then they mention they have "prior obligations" that day. So, they have something else they need to do before the ceremony. That makes me think they might not be able to attend the ceremony because of these prior commitments. Wait, but if they have prior obligations, doesn't that mean they can't attend the ceremony? So, saying they "deserve" to attend because of prior obligations seems contradictory. It's like saying, "I should be there because I can't be there." That doesn't make much sense. Maybe they're trying to justify their absence by saying they have prior obligations, but then they're also claiming they deserve to attend. That feels a bit conflicting. It's almost like they're trying to have it both ways: they want to attend but also have reasons why they can't. I wonder if there's a better way to communicate this. Instead of saying they "deserve" to attend because of prior obligations, maybe they should explain their situation more clearly. For example, "I have prior obligations that day, so I won't be able to attend the ceremony." That way, it's straightforward and doesn't imply a sense of entitlement or conflict. Also, the word "deserve" carries a lot of weight. It suggests that they feel they are owed the opportunity to attend, which might not be the best approach if they have prior commitments. It could come off as dismissive of the event or the people organizing it. Perhaps it's better to focus on the fact that they have prior obligations and that they're unable to attend, rather than framing it as something they "deserve." That way, it's more about their circumstances and less about their entitlement. It might be more effective to communicate the situation clearly without implying a sense of entitlement.
